uncited: Multi-view projection voxelization generates a volumetric representation of a triangle mesh by rasterizing the geometry from multiple camera viewpoints, typically aligned with the principal axes of the scene's bounding box.

It differs from [Single 2D Projection Voxelization](3482-single-2d-projection-voxelization.md) by using multiple views to cover all surface normals, and from [3D Grid Rasterization](903-3d-grid-rasterization.md) by relying on standard GPU rasterization pipelines rather than explicit 3D grid traversal.
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of projecting 3D geometry onto 2D planes and aggregating the resulting fragments into a 3D voxel grid.
**Camera Configuration:** Orthographic cameras are positioned along specific axes (e.g., X, Y, Z) looking towards the scene's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB).
**Rasterization:** Triangles are rasterized into 2D buffers (sheet buffers) or directly into a 3D texture.
**Aggregation:** Fragments from different views are merged into the final voxel grid.
This is often an atomic "OR" operation for occupancy or a blending operation for attributes.
The aggregation ensures that if a voxel is hit by any view, it is marked as occupied [Parent, G].
**Parameter:** $L$: Number of depth layers in the cost volume.

Multi-view projection voxelization is a foundational technique in computer graphics for converting triangle meshes into voxel grids for volume rendering, ray marching, and neural radiance fields (NeRF).
The approach leverages the efficiency of GPU rasterization pipelines, which are highly optimized for 2D triangle projection, to bypass the computational complexity of explicit 3D intersection tests.

The use of multiple views (typically three orthogonal axes) was established to solve the "shadow" problem where single-view projections fail to capture surfaces facing away from the camera or those at grazing angles.
The technique has evolved to include efficient memory layouts like 2D worksheets for 3D data compression and iterative refinement for multi-view stereo consistency.
